9: 
10: # create-benchmark
11: 
12: > Turn a benchmark that already ran into documentation an operator can find, then scaffold the input fixtures a benchmark lane needs before it runs, never running or scoring the benchmark itself.
13: 
14: ---
15: 
16: ## 1. AT A GLANCE
17: 
18: | Aspect | What you get |
19: |---|---|
20: | **Use it for** | Authoring benchmark documentation and input artifacts across two families |
21: | **Invoke with** | `/create:benchmark`, "benchmark-report.md", "behavior benchmark" |
22: | **Works on** | Completed benchmark runs and bake-offs, plus the input fixtures a benchmark lane needs before it runs |
23: | **Produces** | Ten-section benchmark reports, package indexes, machine-contract scenario files. Never a rubric, scorer or runner |
24: 
25: ---
26: 
27: ## 2. OVERVIEW
28: 
29: ### Why This Skill Exists
30: 
31: A benchmark finishes inside a spec packet. The result lives three folders deep in an `evidence/` directory, so the next person who touches the MCP code cannot find why a default exists without remembering which packet ran the benchmark. A second gap opens before a benchmark runs at all. Deep-loop modes need stable input fixtures and an index. Hand-rolling those inputs invites exactly the kind of scoring logic that should stay lane-owned. Two distinct benchmark families each have their own package shape. Conflating them breaks the thing the next run depends on.
32: 
33: ### What It Does
34: 
35: `create-benchmark` authors documentation and input artifacts for two benchmark families. MCP promotion writes a `benchmark-report.md` and a `source.md` that move a shipped spec packet's results into a skill's `mcp-server/benchmarks/` tree. Behavior benchmarks get a `behavior-benchmark/` package of scenario contracts for a deep-loop mode. The skill never runs a benchmark and never writes a scorer or rubric. Those stay lane-owned. Start with the `/create:benchmark` command. The family router in `ROUTER.md` section 3 decides which family shape applies. It is the required first stop before authoring anything.
36: 
37: ### The Family Capability Layer
38: 
39: | Family | What it measures | What the skill knows how to operate |
40: |---|---|---|
41: | **MCP promotion** (`shared`) | retrieval, quality, runtime or throughput of a shipped MCP stack | a `benchmark-report.md` and a `source.md` inside `<skill>/mcp-server/benchmarks/benchmark-<date>/` |
42: | **Behavior** (`behavior_benchmark`) | executor-model behavior at a deep-loop mode's invocation surface | a `behavior-benchmark/` package of scenario contracts at `<mode>/behavior-benchmark/` |
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 3. QUICK START
47: 
48: **Step 1: Invoke it.** Run `/create:benchmark` or read `ROUTER.md` section 3 to route to a family first.
49: 
50: **Step 2: Route before you write anything.**
51: 
52: ```text
53: Measurable MCP surface + shipped spec packet with accepted ADRs + stable fixture?
54:   YES -> MCP promotion (SKILL.md section 3-8)
55:   NO  -> check behavior families (ROUTER.md section 3 table)
56: ```
57: 
58: The block is the family router in miniature. MCP promotion is the flagship command-driven family.
59: 
60: **Step 3: Verify before you rely on it.**
61: 
62: ```bash
63: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/scripts/validate_document.py \
64:   mcp-server/benchmarks/benchmark-2026-07-06/benchmark-report.md --type readme
65: ```
66: 
67: Expected: zero blocking issues once the ten required sections are filled in.
68: 
69: ---
70: 
71: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
72: 
73: The flagship family, MCP promotion, runs a fixed sequence.
74: 
75: 1. Confirm the promotion gate first: an accepted decision, a stable headline, a stable fixture and replay commands.
76: 2. Classify the task as a re-run or a retirement when the headline repeats, otherwise as a first-time promotion.
77: 3. Confirm the target skill actually has `mcp-server/`.
78: 4. Create or update the benchmarks index.
79: 5. Choose the `benchmark-YYYY-MM-DD/` folder using the execution date.
80: 6. Copy the source artifacts starting with the aggregate CSV.
81: 7. Write `benchmark-report.md` from the fixed ten-section structure.
82: 8. Write `source.md` as a lean wayfinding pointer back to the spec packet.
83: 9. Update the README index row.
84: 10. Validate.
85: 
86: Behavior benchmarks follow the same authoring-not-running shape. The family's package layout is documented in its own `SKILL.md` section (9) and its own guide under `references/`.
87: 
88: ### Key Concept: Authoring Never Crosses Into Scoring
89: 
90: Every family stops at the same boundary. It writes down what a benchmark measured or what a benchmark needs before it can run. It never writes the thing that decides pass or fail.
91: 
92: ---
93: 
94: ## 5. INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION
95: 
96: ### When To Use This Skill
97: 
98: Reach for this packet when a benchmark already ran and shipped inside a spec packet with an accepted decision record, when a deep-loop mode needs a behavior-benchmark package, when a consuming skill needs its `mcp-server/benchmarks/README.md` index established or updated.
99: 
100: Skip it when the benchmark is still in-flight, is a single unreplayable data point or the real ask is a release note (`create-changelog`) or an audit of benchmark markdown that already exists (`create-quality-control`).
101: 
102: ### Related Skills
103: 
104: | Skill | Relationship |
105: |---|---|
106: | `create-changelog` | Owns a benchmark headline as a release-note row. `create-benchmark` owns the full promotion folder |
107: | `create-quality-control` | Owns auditing or scoring benchmark markdown that already exists, without authoring a new family artifact |
108:

110: 
111: ## 6. TROUBLESHOOTING
112: 
113: | What you see | Why | Fix |
114: |---|---|---|
115: | Validator flags a document-type mismatch | `benchmark-report.md` was checked with the wrong `--type` | Pass `--type readme` (or the closer-matching type) and re-run |
116: | A re-run created a second dated folder | The re-run confirmed the same headline instead of updating in place | Delete the new folder. Add a `Re-run YYYY-MM-DD` note to the existing `benchmark-report.md` instead |
117: | The wrong family template got copied | The family router in `ROUTER.md` section 3 was skipped | Re-route through the family table before authoring anything |
118: 
119: ---
120: 
121: ## 7. FAQ
122: 
123: **Q: Why not just drop the benchmark CSV into the skill's README?**
124: 
125: A: A raw CSV gives a reader a bare number with no methodology and no replay path. The ten sections of `benchmark-report.md` carry the caveats a reader needs, so a reader months later can judge whether the result still holds.
126: 
127: **Q: Why separate families instead of one generic "benchmark" template?**
128: 
129: A: The two families measure genuinely different things: retrieval quality and executor-model behavior each answer a different question. Conflating their package shapes breaks the lane that consumes each one.
130: 
131: **Q: Can this packet run a benchmark for me?**
132: 
133: A: No. It authors documentation and input artifacts only. Execution and scoring stay in the owning lane.
134: 
135: **Q: What if a re-run confirms the same headline as before?**
136: 
137: A: Update the existing `benchmark-report.md` with a `Re-run YYYY-MM-DD` note instead of creating a new dated folder. A new folder is only for a benchmark that actually changes the headline.

10: # create-benchmark
11: 
12: > Turn a benchmark that already ran into documentation an operator can find, then scaffold the input fixtures a benchmark lane needs before it runs, never running or scoring the benchmark itself.
13: 
14: ---
15: 
16: ## 1. AT A GLANCE
17: 
18: | Aspect | What you get |
19: |---|---|
20: | **Use it for** | Authoring benchmark documentation and input artifacts across two families |
21: | **Invoke with** | `/create:benchmark`, "benchmark-report.md", "behavior benchmark" |
22: | **Works on** | Completed benchmark runs and bake-offs, plus the input fixtures a benchmark lane needs before it runs |
23: | **Produces** | Ten-section benchmark reports, package indexes, machine-contract scenario files. Never a rubric, scorer or runner |
24: 
25: ---
26: 
27: ## 2. OVERVIEW
28: 
29: ### Why This Skill Exists
30: 
31: A benchmark finishes inside a spec packet. The result lives three folders deep in an `evidence/` directory, so the next person who touches the MCP code cannot find why a default exists without remembering which packet ran the benchmark. A second gap opens before a benchmark runs at all. Deep-loop modes need stable input fixtures and an index. Hand-rolling those inputs invites exactly the kind of scoring logic that should stay lane-owned. Two distinct benchmark families each have their own package shape. Conflating them breaks the thing the next run depends on.
32: 
33: ### What It Does
34: 
35: `create-benchmark` authors documentation and input artifacts for two benchmark families. MCP promotion writes a `benchmark-report.md` and a `source.md` that move a shipped spec packet's results into a skill's `mcp-server/benchmarks/` tree. Behavior benchmarks get a `behavior-benchmark/` package of scenario contracts for a deep-loop mode. The skill never runs a benchmark and never writes a scorer or rubric. Those stay lane-owned. Start with the `/create:benchmark` command. The family router in `ROUTER.md` section 3 decides which family shape applies. It is the required first stop before authoring anything.
36: 
37: ### The Family Capability Layer
38: 
39: | Family | What it measures | What the skill knows how to operate |
40: |---|---|---|
41: | **MCP promotion** (`shared`) | retrieval, quality, runtime or throughput of a shipped MCP stack | a `benchmark-report.md` and a `source.md` inside `<skill>/mcp-server/benchmarks/benchmark-<date>/` |
42: | **Behavior** (`behavior_benchmark`) | executor-model behavior at a deep-loop mode's invocation surface | a `behavior-benchmark/` package of scenario contracts at `<mode>/behavior-benchmark/` |
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 3. QUICK START
47: 
48: **Step 1: Invoke it.** Run `/create:benchmark` or read `ROUTER.md` section 3 to route to a family first.
49: 
50: **Step 2: Route before you write anything.**
51: 
52: ```text
53: Measurable MCP surface + shipped spec packet with accepted ADRs + stable fixture?
54:   YES -> MCP promotion (SKILL.md section 3-8)
55:   NO  -> check behavior families (ROUTER.md section 3 table)
56: ```
57: 
58: The block is the family router in miniature. MCP promotion is the flagship command-driven family.
59: 
60: **Step 3: Verify before you rely on it.**
61: 
62: ```bash
63: python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/scripts/validate_document.py \
64:   mcp-server/benchmarks/benchmark-2026-07-06/benchmark-report.md --type readme
65: ```
66: 
67: Expected: zero blocking issues once the ten required sections are filled in.
68: 
69: ---
70: 
71: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
72: 
73: The flagship family, MCP promotion, runs a fixed sequence.
74: 
75: 1. Confirm the promotion gate first: an accepted decision, a stable headline, a stable fixture and replay commands.
76: 2. Classify the task as a re-run or a retirement when the headline repeats, otherwise as a first-time promotion.
77: 3. Confirm the target skill actually has `mcp-server/`.
78: 4. Create or update the benchmarks index.
79: 5. Choose the `benchmark-YYYY-MM-DD/` folder using the execution date.
80: 6. Copy the source artifacts starting with the aggregate CSV.
81: 7. Write `benchmark-report.md` from the fixed ten-section structure.
82: 8. Write `source.md` as a lean wayfinding pointer back to the spec packet.
83: 9. Update the README index row.
84: 10. Validate.
85: 
86: Behavior benchmarks follow the same authoring-not-running shape. The family's package layout is documented in its own `SKILL.md` section (9) and its own guide under `references/`.
87: 
88: ### Key Concept: Authoring Never Crosses Into Scoring
89: 
90: Every family stops at the same boundary. It writes down what a benchmark measured or what a benchmark needs before it can run. It never writes the thing that decides pass or fail.
91: 
92: ---
93: 
94: ## 5. INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION
95: 
96: ### When To Use This Skill
97: 
98: Reach for this packet when a benchmark already ran and shipped inside a spec packet with an accepted decision record, when a deep-loop mode needs a behavior-benchmark package, when a consuming skill needs its `mcp-server/benchmarks/README.md` index established or updated.
99: 
100: Skip it when the benchmark is still in-flight, is a single unreplayable data point or the real ask is a release note (`create-changelog`) or an audit of benchmark markdown that already exists (`create-quality-control`).
101: 
102: ### Related Skills
103: 
104: | Skill | Relationship |
105: |---|---|
106: | `create-changelog` | Owns a benchmark headline as a release-note row. `create-benchmark` owns the full promotion folder |
107: | `create-quality-control` | Owns auditing or scoring benchmark markdown that already exists, without authoring a new family artifact |
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: ## 6. TROUBLESHOOTING
112: 
113: | What you see | Why | Fix |
114: |---|---|---|
115: | Validator flags a document-type mismatch | `benchmark-report.md` was checked with the wrong `--type` | Pass `--type readme` (or the closer-matching type) and re-run |
116: | A re-run created a second dated folder | The re-run confirmed the same headline instead of updating in place | Delete the new folder. Add a `Re-run YYYY-MM-DD` note to the existing `benchmark-report.md` instead |
117: | The wrong family template got copied | The family router in `ROUTER.md` section 3 was skipped | Re-route through the family table before authoring anything |
118: 
119: ---
120: 
121: ## 7. FAQ
122: 
123: **Q: Why not just drop the benchmark CSV into the skill's README?**
124: 
125: A: A raw CSV gives a reader a bare number with no methodology and no replay path. The ten sections of `benchmark-report.md` carry the caveats a reader needs, so a reader months later can judge whether the result still holds.
126: 
127: **Q: Why separate families instead of one generic "benchmark" template?**
128: 
129: A: The two families measure genuinely different things: retrieval quality and executor-model behavior each answer a different question. Conflating their package shapes breaks the lane that consumes each one.
130: 
131: **Q: Can this packet run a benchmark for me?**
132: 
133: A: No. It authors documentation and input artifacts only. Execution and scoring stay in the owning lane.
134: 
135: **Q: What if a re-run confirms the same headline as before?**
136: 
137: A: Update the existing `benchmark-report.md` with a `Re-run YYYY-MM-DD` note instead of creating a new dated folder. A new folder is only for a benchmark that actually changes the headline.
138:

148: 
149: ---

151: ## 9. RELATED DOCUMENTS

156: | [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md) | Machine router: intent map, resource map and loading levels |
157: | [`references/shared/README.md`](./references/shared/README.md) | Overflow route-map: case studies, the report worked example and common pitfalls |
158: | [`references/behavior-benchmark/behavior-benchmark-guide.md`](./references/behavior-benchmark/behavior-benchmark-guide.md) | End-to-end guide for authoring a `behavior-benchmark` package |
159: | [`assets/shared/benchmark-report-template.md`](./assets/shared/benchmark-report-template.md) | Template for the ten-section `benchmark-report.md` |
160: | [`assets/shared/source-template.md`](./assets/shared/source-template.md) | Template for the `source.md` wayfinding file |

122: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS: AUTHORING WORKFLOW
123: 
124: Complete these steps in order after the spec packet ships.
125: 
126: Before naming a folder, run label, fixture, or report, validate its resolved path or slug. Do not pass machine keys such as `behavior_benchmark` as filesystem names.

132: 1. **Confirm the promotion gate.** Read `decision-record.md`, `implementation-summary.md`, and benchmark evidence. Require an accepted decision, stable headline and fixture, replay commands, and a defensible winner or explicit provisional status.

146: - Write the load-bearing insight and caveats before recommendations.
147: - Validate before adding or finalizing the README index row.

152: | Skill-local file | Source in spec packet |
153: | --- | --- |

163: 
164: Keep this fixed ten-section `benchmark-report.md` structure; never merge, reorder, or omit:
165: 
166: 1. **HEADLINE / OVERVIEW**: one-line winner or status plus key metric.
167: 2. **AGGREGATE RESULTS**: one row per candidate, headline metrics, and verdict.
168: 3. **METHODOLOGY**: fixture, sample size, pipeline, environment, and replay context.
169: 4. **PER-CANDIDATE PROFILES**: RAM, disk, dim, release, strengths, and weaknesses.
170: 5. **PROCESS NOTES**: what was tried, what failed, and why.
171: 6. **FINDINGS**: unique wins, universal floor and ceiling, mismatch analysis, and load-bearing insight.
172: 7. **CAVEATS**: single-run signal, fixture limits, stack-level confounds, schema migration cost, reranker/runtime confounds.
173: 8. **RECOMMENDATIONS**: Tier 1 apply now, Tier 2 validate first, Tier 3 future.
174: 9. **REPRODUCIBILITY**: exact replay commands plus expected wall-clock.
175: 10. **CROSS-LINKS**: sibling MCP benchmarks, authoritative spec packet, follow-on packets.
176: 
177: For an empty section, retain its header and write: `Not applicable to this bench. Reason: ...`
178: 
179: ### Report Style
180: 
181: - Match sk-doc reference quality and frontmatter.
182: - Use H2 numbered headers with ALL CAPS section names.
183: - Use tables for data and fenced code blocks for verbatim commands.
184: - Keep slugs and anchors stable across revisions.
185: - Do not paste the full spec packet decision trail into the report.
186: - Do not compare numeric results across different MCP stacks as if equivalent.
187:

189: 
190: Use this shape near the top of the report:
191: 
192: ```markdown
193: # <topic> bake-off: <date>
194: 
195: > Headline: `<winner>` + <pipeline-config> is the production default for `<MCP-stack>`.
196: > <primary-metric> <numeric-result>, <secondary-metric> <numeric-result>. Closes packet <packet-id>.
197: ```

199: If the load-bearing insight differs from the winner, state it in Sections 1 and 6.

203: ## 6. DATE AND NAMING CONVENTION
204: 
205: ### Folder Names
206: 
207: One grammar governs every benchmark family. A run folder is named:
208: 
209: ```text
210: <YYYY-MM-DD>--<subject>--<variant>/
211: ```
212: 
213: - Fields are separated by a double hyphen. Words inside a field use a single hyphen.
214: - Lowercase ASCII only. No underscores, no dots, no capitals.
215: - The date is the **execution** date, not the authoring or publication date. Publication date belongs in
216:   the report body, where a reader can see both.
217: - `<subject>` names the corpus the run measured: `manual-testing-playbook`, `mcp-retrieval`,
218:   `model-eval`, `behavior`.
219: - `<variant>` names what most distinguishes the run. For a **feature-scoped** run — one validating a
220:   single feature or scenario group rather than comparing executors — name the feature (e.g. `goal-hook`),
221:   not the model; the model/executor is recorded inside the report (`model`/`providerModel` fields, the
222:   byline, the command shape), so the folder stays legible when the same feature is later re-validated on
223:   another model. For an **executor-scoped** run — one whose point is which model and effort produced it —
224:   name the executor identity as `<runtime>-<model>-<effort>`; use `model-comparison` when it compares
225:   several, or a short topic slug when no model applies.
226: - Model versions flatten their dots: `glm-5.2` becomes `glm-5-2`, `kimi-2.7` becomes `kimi-2-7`. A dot
227:   is rejected by the run-label validator, so this is a hard requirement rather than a style preference.
228: - Two runs of the same subject and variant on one day disambiguate with a trailing topic field.
229: 
230: Examples:
231: 
232: ```text
233: 2026-07-29--manual-testing-playbook--goal-hook/                 # feature-scoped: names the feature, model recorded inside
234: 2026-07-26--manual-testing-playbook--cursor-grok-4-5-high-fast/ # executor-scoped: names the model+effort that ran it
235: 2026-07-26--manual-testing-playbook--model-comparison/
236: 2026-05-18--mcp-retrieval--bge-confirmation/
237: ```
238: 
239: **One exception: `baseline/`.** The frozen comparison anchor keeps its name. It is not a run, it is the
240: before-snapshot every run is measured against, and the archiver refuses it as a run label for exactly
241: that reason. Dating it would make it look like one run among many.
242: 
243: Authored scenario contracts are not run folders. Behavior families keep their
244: `<PREFIX>-NNN-<slug>.md` scenario identifiers, which name a scenario rather than a directory. Any run
245: those families produce follows the grammar above.

249: Use readable long-form dates in prose, such as `May 18, 2026`.

277:

282: 5. Preserve retired benchmark folders.
283: 6. Validate authored markdown before delivery.

316: ## 9. BEHAVIOR BENCHMARK PACKAGES
317: 
318: Behavior benchmarks are run contracts, not numeric MCP bake-offs. They specify

164: Keep this fixed ten-section `benchmark-report.md` structure; never merge, reorder, or omit:

14: 
15: # Behavior Benchmark Authoring Guide
16: 
17: Overflow depth for authoring a `behavior-benchmark` package. This guide walks the
18: authoring path end to end and points at the three templates and the normative
19: framework. It does NOT restate the measurement contract: the five-dimension
20: rubric, terminal buckets, budget formula, entry-surface and clarity enums, and the
21: per-package ID-prefix table live once in
22: [`../../../../system-deep-loop/shared/behavior-benchmark/framework.md`](../../../../system-deep-loop/shared/behavior-benchmark/framework.md).
23: Where this guide and that framework diverge, the framework prevails.
24: 
25: ---
26: 
27: ## 1. OVERVIEW: WHAT A BEHAVIOR BENCHMARK IS
28: 
29: A behavior benchmark measures what an executor **model** does when a deep-loop
30: mode's invocation surface is triggered with a realistic user prompt: whether it
31: dispatches the mode's LEAF agent instead of absorbing the role, whether it halts
32: for one consolidated setup question when the prompt is under-specified, whether it
33: respects the mode's invariants, and how long each of those takes relative to a
34: Claude reference leg. It is a package of run contracts, not a numeric bake-off.
35: 
36: Each behavior benchmark is carried by exactly one deep-loop mode-packet, at
37: `<mode>/behavior-benchmark/`, and is governed by the single shared framework.
38: Sibling modes each carry their own package; they share the framework, the runner,
39: and the scoring so results stay comparable across modes.
40: 
41: ### When to Use
42: 
43: - You are authoring a `<mode>/behavior-benchmark/` package: its index, scenario contracts, and baseline.
44: - You are extending an existing package with a new scenario cell.
45: - You need the scenario-matrix design, package layout, naming rules, or validation steps.
46: 
47: If the task is promoting MCP numbers, use the MCP-promotion path in `../SKILL.md`. If the task is specifying executor behavior for a deep-loop mode, use this guide.
48: 
49: ### How it differs from an MCP promotion benchmark
50: 
51: The other benchmark family this packet authors — see [`../../SKILL.md`](../../SKILL.md)
52: sections 3 through 8 — promotes a completed MCP retrieval or runtime bake-off into
53: a consuming skill's `mcp-server/benchmarks/` folder with a ten-section
54: `benchmark-report.md`. The two families are distinct and must not be conflated:
55: 
56: | Dimension | MCP promotion benchmark | Behavior benchmark |
57: | --- | --- | --- |
58: | What it measures | Retrieval, quality, runtime, or throughput numbers from a shipped MCP stack | Executor-model behavior at a deep-loop mode's invocation surface |
59: | Lives at | `<skill>/mcp-server/benchmarks/benchmark-<YYYY-MM-DD>/` | `<mode>/behavior-benchmark/` |
60: | Central artifact | Ten-section `benchmark-report.md` plus `source.md` | `behavior-benchmark.md` index plus per-scenario contracts plus a baseline |
61: | Governing contract | The report contract in `../SKILL.md` | The shared `framework.md` |
62: | Evidence location | The dated folder is the curated surface; audit trail in the spec packet | The package holds the contract; run evidence lands in the executing spec-packet phase |
63: 
64: ---
65: 
66: ## 2. PACKAGE LAYOUT
67: 
68: Author this shape inside the owning deep-loop mode-packet:
69: 
70: ```text
71: <mode>/behavior-benchmark/
72: ├── behavior-benchmark.md          # the package index (scenario table + axis coverage)
73: ├── scenarios/
74: │   ├── <PREFIX>-001-<slug>.md     # one machine-contract file per scenario
75: │   ├── <PREFIX>-002-<slug>.md
76: │   └── ...
77: └── baselines/
78:     └── claude-baseline.md         # per-scenario Claude-leg reference checkpoints
79: ```
80: 
81: | File | Required | Template |
82: | --- | --- | --- |
83: | `behavior-benchmark.md` | Yes | [`../../assets/behavior-benchmark/behavior-benchmark-index-template.md`](../../assets/behavior-benchmark/behavior-benchmark-index-template.md) |
84: | `scenarios/<PREFIX>-NNN-<slug>.md` | One per scenario | [`../../assets/behavior-benchmark/behavior-benchmark-scenario-template.md`](../../assets/behavior-benchmark/behavior-benchmark-scenario-template.md) |
85: | `baselines/claude-baseline.md` | Yes | [`../../assets/behavior-benchmark/behavior-benchmark-baseline-template.md`](../../assets/behavior-benchmark/behavior-benchmark-baseline-template.md) |
86: 
87: Fixtures, lane-configs, transcripts, result JSONs, and scorecards are NOT shipped
88: in this package. The executing spec-packet phase provisions the fixtures and holds
89: the run evidence. The package is the contract; the packet is the proof.
90: 
91: ---
92: 
93: ## 3. NAMING CONVENTIONS
94: 
95: New packages follow the sk-doc filesystem convention. The shipped legacy
96: `deep-review/behavior-benchmark/` package remains a current underscore-path
97: reference until its owning rename phase.
98: 
99: - **Package directory**: `behavior-benchmark`, directly under the mode-packet.
100: - **Index file**: `behavior-benchmark.md`, matching the directory.
101: - **Scenario files**: `<PREFIX>-NNN-<slug>.md` — an uppercase three-letter ID
102:   prefix, a zero-padded three-digit number, then a lowercase-hyphen slug, for
103:   example `RVB-001-auto-run-specified.md`. The `NNN` is contiguous from `001`.
104: - **Baseline file**: `baselines/claude-baseline.md`.
105: - **ID prefix**: three uppercase letters, unique per package. The framework fixes
106:   `ACB` (ai-council), `RSB` (research), and `RVB` (review).
107:   A new mode extends that table with its own prefix and declares it
108:   in the index OVERVIEW. Confirm the prefix is not already taken before assigning it.
109: 
110: ---
111: 
112: ## 4. AUTHORING WORKFLOW
113: 
114: Complete these steps in order.
115: 
116: 1. **Read the framework.** Load
117:    [`../../../../system-deep-loop/shared/behavior-benchmark/framework.md`](../../../../system-deep-loop/shared/behavior-benchmark/framework.md)
118:    in full: the scenario contract schema, the five-dimension rubric, the terminal
119:    buckets, the budget formula, and the ID-prefix table. It is the authority for
120:    every field the scenario template leaves as a placeholder.
121: 2. **Read the owning mode contract.** Load the mode's `SKILL.md` and pull its
122:    invariants, its LEAF agent name, its invocation surface (command and natural
123:    forms), and the adjacent modes it must decline work for. These become the
124:    distinctive cells.
125: 3. **Assign the ID prefix and confirm the mode value.** Pick an unused three-letter
126:    prefix. If the mode value is not already in the framework's `mode` enum, that is
127:    a framework extension to declare in the index OVERVIEW, grounded in where the
128:    shipped mode already carries the value.
129: 4. **Design the scenario matrix.** Cover the entry-surface and clarity axes
130:    deliberately, and isolate each distinctive invariant and each boundary in its
131:    own cell. See section 5.
132: 5. **Write the index.** Copy the index template to `behavior-benchmark.md`, fill
133:    the OVERVIEW, SCENARIO TABLE, AXIS COVERAGE, EXECUTION, and RELATED RESOURCES
134:    sections, and delete the availability blockquote unless the invocation surface
135:    is planned-but-not-built.
136: 6. **Write one scenario file per row.** Copy the scenario template per row, then
137:    keep exactly ONE of its two JSON blocks:
138:    - the schema-v1 core for the research/review/ai-council/context packages, or
139:    - the schema-v2 block (`"schema_version": 2` with `command_topology`, direct-dispatch targets, `postconditions`, and `boundary`) for command, direct-tool/plugin, and conformance families that need direct-dispatch targets, postcondition probes, or a fixture boundary.
140: 
141:    Delete the block you are not using. The remaining fenced json block is the
142:    machine contract the runner parses; keep its field order. Fill Rationale,
143:    Pass shape, and Failure modes as scoring context. Keep every row in the index
144:    table and its scenario file in exact sync.
145: 7. **Write the baseline.** Copy the baseline template to
146:    `baselines/claude-baseline.md`. Ship every cell `pending` / `not_captured` if no
147:    Claude leg has run — that is a legitimate ship state, but it is never quotable
148:    as behavior.
149: 8. **Validate.** Run the sk-doc document validator on the index and baseline (see
150:    section 6). Scenario files carry no frontmatter by design; validate them for
151:    structure by confirming the first fenced json block parses and the ID matches
152:    the filename.
153: 9. **Hand fixtures and capture to the executing packet.** The package does not run
154:    itself. The spec-packet phase that executes a round provisions the fixtures,
155:    runs the runner, and files the evidence; only then do the baseline `pending`
156:    cells get replaced and the budgets recomputed.

15: # Behavior Benchmark Authoring Guide
16: 
17: Overflow depth for authoring a `behavior-benchmark` package. This guide walks the
18: authoring path end to end and points at the three templates and the normative
19: framework. It does NOT restate the measurement contract: the five-dimension
20: rubric, terminal buckets, budget formula, entry-surface and clarity enums, and the
21: per-package ID-prefix table live once in
22: [`../../../../system-deep-loop/shared/behavior-benchmark/framework.md`](../../../../system-deep-loop/shared/behavior-benchmark/framework.md).
23: Where this guide and that framework diverge, the framework prevails.
24: 
25: ---
26: 
27: ## 1. OVERVIEW: WHAT A BEHAVIOR BENCHMARK IS
28: 
29: A behavior benchmark measures what an executor **model** does when a deep-loop
30: mode's invocation surface is triggered with a realistic user prompt: whether it
31: dispatches the mode's LEAF agent instead of absorbing the role, whether it halts
32: for one consolidated setup question when the prompt is under-specified, whether it
33: respects the mode's invariants, and how long each of those takes relative to a
34: Claude reference leg. It is a package of run contracts, not a numeric bake-off.
35: 
36: Each behavior benchmark is carried by exactly one deep-loop mode-packet, at
37: `<mode>/behavior-benchmark/`, and is governed by the single shared framework.
38: Sibling modes each carry their own package; they share the framework, the runner,
39: and the scoring so results stay comparable across modes.
40: 
41: ### When to Use
42: 
43: - You are authoring a `<mode>/behavior-benchmark/` package: its index, scenario contracts, and baseline.
44: - You are extending an existing package with a new scenario cell.
45: - You need the scenario-matrix design, package layout, naming rules, or validation steps.
46: 
47: If the task is promoting MCP numbers, use the MCP-promotion path in `../SKILL.md`. If the task is specifying executor behavior for a deep-loop mode, use this guide.
48: 
49: ### How it differs from an MCP promotion benchmark
50: 
51: The other benchmark family this packet authors — see [`../../SKILL.md`](../../SKILL.md)
52: sections 3 through 8 — promotes a completed MCP retrieval or runtime bake-off into
53: a consuming skill's `mcp-server/benchmarks/` folder with a ten-section
54: `benchmark-report.md`. The two families are distinct and must not be conflated:
55: 
56: | Dimension | MCP promotion benchmark | Behavior benchmark |
57: | --- | --- | --- |
58: | What it measures | Retrieval, quality, runtime, or throughput numbers from a shipped MCP stack | Executor-model behavior at a deep-loop mode's invocation surface |
59: | Lives at | `<skill>/mcp-server/benchmarks/benchmark-<YYYY-MM-DD>/` | `<mode>/behavior-benchmark/` |
60: | Central artifact | Ten-section `benchmark-report.md` plus `source.md` | `behavior-benchmark.md` index plus per-scenario contracts plus a baseline |
61: | Governing contract | The report contract in `../SKILL.md` | The shared `framework.md` |
62: | Evidence location | The dated folder is the curated surface; audit trail in the spec packet | The package holds the contract; run evidence lands in the executing spec-packet phase |
63: 
64: ---
65: 
66: ## 2. PACKAGE LAYOUT
67: 
68: Author this shape inside the owning deep-loop mode-packet:
69: 
70: ```text
71: <mode>/behavior-benchmark/
72: ├── behavior-benchmark.md          # the package index (scenario table + axis coverage)
73: ├── scenarios/
74: │   ├── <PREFIX>-001-<slug>.md     # one machine-contract file per scenario
75: │   ├── <PREFIX>-002-<slug>.md
76: │   └── ...
77: └── baselines/
78:     └── claude-baseline.md         # per-scenario Claude-leg reference checkpoints
79: ```
80: 
81: | File | Required | Template |
82: | --- | --- | --- |
83: | `behavior-benchmark.md` | Yes | [`../../assets/behavior-benchmark/behavior-benchmark-index-template.md`](../../assets/behavior-benchmark/behavior-benchmark-index-template.md) |
84: | `scenarios/<PREFIX>-NNN-<slug>.md` | One per scenario | [`../../assets/behavior-benchmark/behavior-benchmark-scenario-template.md`](../../assets/behavior-benchmark/behavior-benchmark-scenario-template.md) |
85: | `baselines/claude-baseline.md` | Yes | [`../../assets/behavior-benchmark/behavior-benchmark-baseline-template.md`](../../assets/behavior-benchmark/behavior-benchmark-baseline-template.md) |
86: 
87: Fixtures, lane-configs, transcripts, result JSONs, and scorecards are NOT shipped
88: in this package. The executing spec-packet phase provisions the fixtures and holds
89: the run evidence. The package is the contract; the packet is the proof.
90: 
91: ---
92: 
93: ## 3. NAMING CONVENTIONS
94: 
95: New packages follow the sk-doc filesystem convention. The shipped legacy
96: `deep-review/behavior-benchmark/` package remains a current underscore-path
97: reference until its owning rename phase.
98: 
99: - **Package directory**: `behavior-benchmark`, directly under the mode-packet.
100: - **Index file**: `behavior-benchmark.md`, matching the directory.
101: - **Scenario files**: `<PREFIX>-NNN-<slug>.md` — an uppercase three-letter ID
102:   prefix, a zero-padded three-digit number, then a lowercase-hyphen slug, for
103:   example `RVB-001-auto-run-specified.md`. The `NNN` is contiguous from `001`.
104: - **Baseline file**: `baselines/claude-baseline.md`.
105: - **ID prefix**: three uppercase letters, unique per package. The framework fixes
106:   `ACB` (ai-council), `RSB` (research), and `RVB` (review).
107:   A new mode extends that table with its own prefix and declares it
108:   in the index OVERVIEW. Confirm the prefix is not already taken before assigning it.
109: 
110: ---
111: 
112: ## 4. AUTHORING WORKFLOW
113: 
114: Complete these steps in order.
115: 
116: 1. **Read the framework.** Load
117:    [`../../../../system-deep-loop/shared/behavior-benchmark/framework.md`](../../../../system-deep-loop/shared/behavior-benchmark/framework.md)
118:    in full: the scenario contract schema, the five-dimension rubric, the terminal
119:    buckets, the budget formula, and the ID-prefix table. It is the authority for
120:    every field the scenario template leaves as a placeholder.
121: 2. **Read the owning mode contract.** Load the mode's `SKILL.md` and pull its
122:    invariants, its LEAF agent name, its invocation surface (command and natural
123:    forms), and the adjacent modes it must decline work for. These become the
124:    distinctive cells.
125: 3. **Assign the ID prefix and confirm the mode value.** Pick an unused three-letter
126:    prefix. If the mode value is not already in the framework's `mode` enum, that is
127:    a framework extension to declare in the index OVERVIEW, grounded in where the
128:    shipped mode already carries the value.
129: 4. **Design the scenario matrix.** Cover the entry-surface and clarity axes
130:    deliberately, and isolate each distinctive invariant and each boundary in its
131:    own cell. See section 5.
132: 5. **Write the index.** Copy the index template to `behavior-benchmark.md`, fill
133:    the OVERVIEW, SCENARIO TABLE, AXIS COVERAGE, EXECUTION, and RELATED RESOURCES
134:    sections, and delete the availability blockquote unless the invocation surface
135:    is planned-but-not-built.
136: 6. **Write one scenario file per row.** Copy the scenario template per row, then
137:    keep exactly ONE of its two JSON blocks:
138:    - the schema-v1 core for the research/review/ai-council/context packages, or
139:    - the schema-v2 block (`"schema_version": 2` with `command_topology`, direct-dispatch targets, `postconditions`, and `boundary`) for command, direct-tool/plugin, and conformance families that need direct-dispatch targets, postcondition probes, or a fixture boundary.

141:    Delete the block you are not using. The remaining fenced json block is the
142:    machine contract the runner parses; keep its field order. Fill Rationale,
143:    Pass shape, and Failure modes as scoring context. Keep every row in the index
144:    table and its scenario file in exact sync.
145: 7. **Write the baseline.** Copy the baseline template to
146:    `baselines/claude-baseline.md`. Ship every cell `pending` / `not_captured` if no
147:    Claude leg has run — that is a legitimate ship state, but it is never quotable
148:    as behavior.
149: 8. **Validate.** Run the sk-doc document validator on the index and baseline (see
150:    section 6). Scenario files carry no frontmatter by design; validate them for
151:    structure by confirming the first fenced json block parses and the ID matches
152:    the filename.
153: 9. **Hand fixtures and capture to the executing packet.** The package does not run
154:    itself. The spec-packet phase that executes a round provisions the fixtures,
155:    runs the runner, and files the evidence; only then do the baseline `pending`
156:    cells get replaced and the budgets recomputed.

186:

190: 
191: ---

193: ## 6. VALIDATION

196:   shared document validator:
197: 
198:   ```bash
199:   python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/shared/scripts/validate_document.py <file> --type readme
200:   ```
201: 
202: - **Scenario files** ship without frontmatter by design (they open at the

15: # Benchmark Adoption Case Studies
16: 
17: Two adoptions teach the format from opposite ends: one promoted into a live skill, one deliberately kept archived. Read them when modeling a new benchmark folder or deciding whether a provisional run is ready to promote.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: Each case study records what triggered the adoption decision, the load-bearing insight the folder had to surface, and the lesson for the next author. Case study 1 is a clean promotion backed by many ADRs; case study 2 is a correctly-formatted run that was deliberately never promoted because its headline was a single-run signal. Neither folder is on disk any more, so both read as narrative. The lesson outlives the artifact, which is itself worth noticing when you decide what to write down.
24: 
25: ### When to Use
26: 
27: - Modeling a new benchmark folder on an adoption that worked.
28: - Deciding whether a provisional run is ready to promote or should stay archived.
29: 
30: ---
31: 
32: ## 2. CASE STUDY 1: TEXT-EMBEDDER BAKE-OFF (May 17, 2026)
33: 
34: The folder lived in the memory MCP server's skill tree and went with that server when it was decommissioned. What follows is the narrative, not a link.
35: 
36: The bake-off compared six text embedders against a deterministic paraphrase-recall fixture. Twelve ADRs landed in a single day across rollbacks, fixture surgery and a retrieval-rescue pivot. The spec packet ended with the winning embedder plus retrieval-rescue layer as the production default.
37: 
38: **What triggered adoption**: production ran on a different embedder than the schema fallback, and the rescue layer was default-on. Every future operator inside that MCP code would need to know which embedder was active, why and what fixture closed the gate. Promoting a curated entry point gave the next operator a sub-minute orientation.
39: 
40: **The load-bearing insight was not the headline winner.** The most valuable finding was that the retrieval-rescue layer contributed more lift to recall than any embedder swap measured in the bake-off. Pre-rescue, no candidate reached the PASS gate. Post-rescue, scores climbed by three to six points depending on the candidate. Future embedder swaps must measure with the rescue layer on against that baseline. Putting that at the top of a skill-local folder kept it one click from anyone in the code, instead of buried in ADR-010 of a spec packet they would have to know existed.
41: 
42: **Lesson**: A benchmark folder pays off most when the spec packet has many ADRs supporting one curated headline. Promote a `runtime-measurements.md` companion only when the runtime profile is part of the decision (RAM headroom, daemon residency, cold-load time).
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 3. CASE STUDY 2: CODE-EMBEDDER BAKE-OFF (experimental coco-index MCP, May 18, 2026)
47: 
48: Path: `.opencode/specs/z-future/code-graph-and-cocoindex/backup/mcp-coco-index/mcp-server/benchmarks/benchmark-2026-05-18/`
49: 
50: This bake-off belonged to an experimental `mcp-coco-index` server, not a live shipped skill. The run stayed provisional and the server was parked, so the folder lived under `specs/z-future/` rather than in a skill tree. It is preserved here as a teaching example of a correctly-formatted but deliberately un-promoted run.

15: # Benchmark Folder Common Pitfalls
16: 
17: The mistakes that most often make a skill-local benchmark folder drift from its spec packet or break the convention. Check this list when reviewing a drafted `benchmark-report.md` or when a promoted report no longer matches the packet it came from.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: Each row names a mistake, why it breaks the skill-local surface, and the correct fix. The two case studies in [case-studies.md](case-studies.md) show real adoptions that avoided these traps; the ALWAYS/NEVER rules and authority hierarchy that back them live in [`../../SKILL.md`](../../SKILL.md) §7.
24: 
25: ### When to Use
26: 
27: - Reviewing a drafted `benchmark-report.md` or benchmark folder.
28: - A promoted report no longer matches the packet it came from.
29: - A re-run or retirement is about to change an existing folder.
30: 
31: ---
32: 
33: ## 2. COMMON MISTAKES
34: 
35: | Mistake | Why It Breaks | Correct Fix |
36: |---|---|---|
37: | Promoting before the spec packet ADR is accepted | Skill-local report drifts from the eventual decision | Wait for ADR ratification before authoring `benchmark-report.md` |
38: | Omitting the load-bearing insight | Future operators miss the finding that matters most | State the non-obvious finding explicitly in Section 1 "What Shipped" and in Section 6 "Findings" |
39: | Naming folders by doc-authoring date | Folder date no longer matches evidence date | Always use the bench execution date for the folder name |
40: | Deleting retired benchmark folders | Audit trail is lost | Mark RETIRED in `README.md`; keep the folder |
41: | Cross-referencing numbers between skills | Stacks differ; numbers are not comparable | Add a "Stack distinction" line in Caveats; link to the sibling README but do not compare figures |
42: | Creating a new dated folder for a re-run that confirms the winner | Pollutes the index with redundant folders | Update the existing `benchmark-report.md` with a "Re-run YYYY-MM-DD" section |
43: | Writing a ten-section report without a source.md | Readers cannot find the audit trail | Always author source.md; use the `source-template.md` scaffold |
44: 
45: ---
46: 
47: *See [case-studies.md](case-studies.md) for adoptions that avoided these mistakes, and [`../../SKILL.md`](../../SKILL.md) for the authoritative workflow and rules.*

20: ### Location & Naming
21: 
22: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/assets/`
23: 
24: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with the appropriate extension
25: 
26: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
27: |---------------|-----------------|
28: | `frontmatter-templates.md` | `FrontmatterTemplates.md` (PascalCase) |
29: | `config-examples.yaml` | `config_examples.yaml` (snake_case) |

31: | `emoji-reference.md` | `emojiReference.md` (camelCase) |
32: 
33: ### When to Create Assets
34: 
35: **Create an asset file when:**
36: - Templates users apply repeatedly
37: - Reference data >50 lines and self-contained
38: - Multiple examples of same pattern exist
39: - Lookup tables or decision matrices needed
40: - Template variations for different scenarios

43: - Content <30 lines

65: - Document templates (SKILL.md, commands, knowledge files)

121: - Integration guides

125: ## 3. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
126: 
127: ### Title and Intro
128: 
129: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
130: 
131: ```markdown
132: ---
133: title: [Title]
134: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
135: trigger_phrases:
136:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
137:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
138:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
139: importance_tier: normal
140: contextType: general
141: version: 1.0.0.0
142: ---
143: 
144: # [Title]
145: 
146: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
147: 
148: \## 1. OVERVIEW
149: 
150: ### Purpose
151: 
152: [Why this asset exists]
153: 
154: ### Usage
155: 
156: [How to use this asset - copy instructions, customization notes]
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: \## 2. [Content Section]
161: 
162: [The actual template/checklist/snippet content]
163: 
164: ---
165: 
166: ## N. Related Resources (optional, if present must be last)
167: 
168: [Links to related files]
169: 
170: ```
171: 
172: Every asset file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content, `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, and `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
173: 
174: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and OVERVIEW section.**
175: > The intro is a hook. OVERVIEW provides the details.
176: 
177: #### GOOD Intro Structure
178: 
179: ```markdown
180: # Git Commit Templates
181: 
182: Copy the template that matches the change, fill the fields, and commit.
183: 
184: \## 1. OVERVIEW
185: 
186: ### Purpose
187: 
188: Uniform messages let a reader scan history by intent instead of by author.
189: 
190: ### Usage
191: 
192: Copy the appropriate template based on commit type...
193: 
194: ---
195: 
196: \## 2. COMMIT TEMPLATES
197: ...
198: ```
199: 
200: #### BAD Intro Structure (too long, has subsections)
201: 
202: ```markdown
203: # Git Commit Templates
204: 
205: Copy-paste templates for creating well-structured commit messages.
206: 
207: ### Core Principle    ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
208: Atomic commits with clear intent = maintainable history.
209: 
210: ### When to Use       ← WRONG: This belongs in OVERVIEW section!
211: - Creating new features
212: - Fixing bugs
213: 
214: ---
215: ```
216: 
217: ### Intro vs OVERVIEW Content Placement
218: 
219: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | OVERVIEW Section       |
220: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------- |
221: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat)    |
222: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
223: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
224: | How to copy/customize | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
225: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
226: | Any H2/H3 subsections | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES                  |

305: ## 5. LOGIC REPRESENTATION PATTERNS
306: 
307: **Purpose**: Guidelines for representing logic, workflows, and decision trees in asset files using structured formats instead of prose.
308: 
309: **Why Structured Logic?**
310: - **Clarity**: Executable-style logic is easier to understand than prose
311: - **AI-Friendly**: LLMs parse structured logic better than narrative descriptions
312: - **Maintainability**: Changes to logic are more visible in structured formats
313: - **Consistency**: Same patterns across all asset files
314: 
315: ### When to Use Each Format
316: 
317: **Use Python Pseudo-Code When:**
318: - Complex branching logic (multiple IF/ELIF/ELSE conditions)
319: - Function/method definitions with clear inputs/outputs
320: - State management or algorithmic processes
321: - Validation or transformation logic
322: - Examples: Mode detection, validation pipelines, decision functions
323: 
324: **Use YAML Structures When:**
325: - Configuration data (settings, options, parameters)
326: - Pipeline definitions (multi-step workflows with clear phases)
327: - Hierarchical workflows (nested processes)
328: - Metadata structures (categorization, tagging)
329: - Examples: Workflow definitions, configuration templates, feature matrices
330: 
331: **Use Markdown Decision Trees When:**
332: - Simple branching logic (2-5 branches)
333: - Visual flow representation (user-facing paths)
334: - Classification systems (type determination)
335: - Quick decision guides
336: - Examples: Document type selection, frontmatter requirements
337: 
338: **Keep Markdown Prose When:**
339: - Explanatory text and conceptual overviews
340: - Narrative examples with context
341: - Best practices guidance
342: - Introductions and summaries
343:

345: 
346: ## 6. DECISION LOGIC EXAMPLES
347: 
348: **Purpose**: Demonstrate how to convert markdown prose into structured decision logic.
349: 
350: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Mode Detection
351: 
352: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
353: ```markdown
354: Check user input for mode indicators:
355: - If "$quick" is present, use quick mode with auto-scaling depth
356: - If "$ticket" is present, use ticket mode with depth 10
357: - Otherwise, use interactive mode with depth 10
358: ```
359: 
360: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
361: ```python
362: def detect_mode(request):
363:     """Detect execution mode from user request markers"""
364: 
365:     if '$quick' in request:
366:         mode = 'quick'
367:         depth = 'auto_scale_1_to_5'
368:     elif '$ticket' in request:
369:         mode = 'ticket'
370:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
371:     else:
372:         # DEFAULT TO INTERACTIVE
373:         mode = 'interactive'
374:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
375: 
376:     return mode, depth
377: ```
378: 
379: ### Markdown Decision Tree: Frontmatter Requirements
380: 
381: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
382: ```markdown
383: Different document types have different frontmatter requirements:
384: - SKILL.md files must have frontmatter with name, description, allowed-tools, and version
385: - Command files must have frontmatter with description and argument-hint
386: - Skill reference/asset files must have the 5-field block
387: - Knowledge files outside skill folders should not have frontmatter
388: - Spec files typically don't have frontmatter
389: ```
390: 
391: **After (Markdown Decision Tree)**:
392: ```
393: Document type?
394: ├─> SKILL.md             → MUST have frontmatter (name, description, allowed-tools, version)
395: ├─> Command              → MUST have frontmatter (description, argument-hint, allowed-tools)
396: ├─> Skill Reference/Asset → MUST have the 5-field block (title, description,
397: │                           trigger_phrases, importance_tier, contextType)
398: ├─> Knowledge (outside skills) → MUST NOT have frontmatter (remove if present)
399: ├─> Spec                 → SHOULD NOT have frontmatter (suggest removal)
400: └─> README               → No specific requirement (usually none)
401: ```
402: 
403: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Validation Logic
404: 
405: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
406: ```markdown
407: Validate the document structure:
408: 1. Check if required sections exist
409: 2. Verify section ordering is correct
410: 3. Ensure frontmatter is valid (if present)
411: ```
412: 
413: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
414: ```python
415: def validate_document(doc, doc_type):
416:     """Validate document structure and content"""
417: 
418:     errors = []
419: 
420:     # Check required sections
421:     required_sections = get_required_sections(doc_type)
422:     for section in required_sections:
423:         if section not in doc.sections:
424:             errors.append(f"Missing required section: {section}")
425: 
426:     # Verify section ordering
427:     expected_order = get_section_order(doc_type)
428:     actual_order = [s.name for s in doc.sections]
429:     if actual_order != expected_order:
430:         errors.append(f"Section order incorrect. Expected: {expected_order}")
431: 
432:     # Validate frontmatter
433:     if doc.has_frontmatter:
434:         frontmatter_errors = validate_frontmatter(doc.frontmatter, doc_type)
435:         errors.extend(frontmatter_errors)
436: 
437:     return errors
438: ```

442: ## 7. WORKFLOW PATTERNS
443: 
444: **Purpose**: Show how to represent multi-step workflows using YAML structures.
445: 
446: ### YAML Pipeline: Document Creation Workflow
447: 
448: **Before (Markdown List)**:
449: ```markdown
450: 1. Analyze the request and determine document type
451: 2. Select appropriate template
452: 3. Populate template with content
453: 4. Validate structure and content
454: 5. Apply formatting standards
455: 6. Run quality checks
456: ```
457: 
458: **After (YAML Pipeline)**:
459: ```yaml
460: document_creation_workflow:
461:   phase_1_analysis:
462:     action: "Analyze request and determine document type"
463:     output: "Document type classification"
464:     validation: "Type must be one of: SKILL, Command, Knowledge, Spec, README"
465: 
466:   phase_2_template_selection:
467:     action: "Select appropriate template based on document type"
468:     output: "Template file path"
469:     depends_on: "phase_1_analysis"
470: 
471:   phase_3_population:
472:     action: "Populate template with user-provided content"
473:     output: "Draft document with filled sections"
474:     depends_on: "phase_2_template_selection"
475: 
476:   phase_4_validation:
477:     action: "Validate structure, frontmatter, section ordering"
478:     output: "Validation report (errors/warnings)"
479:     depends_on: "phase_3_population"
480: 
481:   phase_5_formatting:
482:     action: "Apply code standards (spacing, headers)"
483:     output: "Formatted document"
484:     depends_on: "phase_4_validation"
485: 
486:   phase_6_quality_check:
487:     action: "Review checklist + run AI quality evaluation"
488:     output: "Quality notes and improvement recommendations"
489:     depends_on: "phase_5_formatting"
490: ```
491: 
492: ### YAML Configuration: Feature Flags
493: 
494: **Before (Markdown Table)**:
495: ```markdown
496: | Feature           | Default | Description                         |
497: | ----------------- | ------- | ----------------------------------- |
498: | strict_validation | true    | Enforce all validation rules        |
499: | auto_fix          | false   | Automatically fix formatting issues |
500: | frontmatter_check | true    | Validate frontmatter per document type |
501: ```
502: 
503: **After (YAML Configuration)**:
504: ```yaml
505: feature_flags:
506:   strict_validation:
507:     default: true
508:     description: "Enforce all validation rules without warnings"
509:     values: [true, false]
510: 
511:   auto_fix:
512:     default: false
513:     description: "Automatically fix formatting issues during validation"
514:     values: [true, false]
515:     warning: "Use with caution - may change document semantics"
516: 
517:   frontmatter_check:
518:     default: true
519:     description: "Validate frontmatter fields per document type"
520:     values: [true, false]
521:     enforcement_level: "error"
522: ```
523: 
524: ### YAML Workflow: Multi-Branch Decision Process
525: 
526: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
527: ```markdown
528: The system should detect when to generate variants:
529: - If user explicitly requests options (shows me options, variations, different approaches)
530: - If complexity is high (7+) and uncertainty signals are present (not sure, what would work)
531: - Otherwise, generate single solution
532: 
533: Variant count depends on complexity:
534: - Simple: 2-3 variants
535: - Standard: 3-5 variants
536: - Complex: 5-10 variants
537: ```
538: 
539: **After (YAML Multi-Branch)**:
540: ```yaml
541: variant_generation_logic:
542:   triggers:
543:     explicit:
544:       keywords: ["show me options", "variations", "different approaches", "multiple designs"]
545:       action: "Generate variants immediately"
546:       priority: "high"
547: 
548:     implicit:
549:       conditions:
550:         - "complexity >= 7"
551:         - "uncertainty_signals present"
552:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work", "best approach"]
553:       action: "Generate variants with uncertainty disclaimer"
554:       priority: "medium"
555: 
556:     default:
557:       action: "Generate single optimal solution"
558:       priority: "low"
559: 
560:   variant_count_guidelines:
561:     simple:
562:       complexity_range: [1, 3]
563:       variant_count: "2-3"
564: 
565:     standard:
566:       complexity_range: [4, 6]
567:       variant_count: "3-5"
568: 
569:     complex:
570:       complexity_range: [7, 10]
571:       variant_count: "5-10"
572: 
573:     user_specified:
574:       action: "Honor user's requested count"
575:       override: true
576: ```

675: ## 9. TEMPLATE GUIDELINES
676: 
677: ### Naming Conventions
678: 
679: **File Names** (kebab-case required):
680: - Format: `[topic]-[type].md`
681: - Use hyphens, not underscores
682: - Lowercase only
683: - Descriptive and specific
684: - Examples:
685:   - ✅ `frontmatter-templates.md`
686:   - ✅ `validation-reference.md`
687:   - ✅ `config-examples.yaml`
688:   - ✅ `packaging-guide.md`
689:   - ❌ `templates.md` (too generic)
690:   - ❌ `FrontmatterTemplates.md` (wrong case)
691:   - ❌ `frontmatter_templates.md` (underscores are not canonical)
692: 
693: **Type-Specific Patterns**:
694: 
695: | Asset Type | Naming Pattern           | Kebab-case Examples          |
696: | ---------- | ------------------------ | ---------------------------- |
697: | Template   | `[content]-templates.md` | `frontmatter-templates.md`   |
698: | Reference  | `[topic]-reference.md`   | `emoji-reference.md`         |
699: | Example    | `[topic]-examples.md`    | `optimization-examples.md`   |
700: | Guide      | `[process]-guide.md`     | `packaging-guide.md`         |
701: | Checklist  | `[topic]-checklist.md`   | `validation-checklist.md`    |
702: 
703: **Section Names**:
704: - Use title case
705: - Be descriptive but concise
706: - Number if sequential: `1. Template Name`
707: 
708: ### Content Organization
709: 
710: **Progressive Disclosure**:
711: 1. **Introduction**: What this is, why it exists (1-2 sentences)
712: 2. **Sections**: Each covers one topic completely
713: 3. **Examples**: Show, don't just tell
714: 4. **Quick Reference**: Summary at end (optional)
715: 
716: **Section Structure**:
717: - **Purpose**: Why this section exists
718: - **Guidelines**: How to use the content
719: - **Template**: Copy-paste starting point
720: - **Example**: Complete working example
721: 
722: ### Formatting Standards
723: 
724: **Code Blocks**:
725: - Always specify language: ` ```yaml `, ` ```markdown `, ` ```bash `
726: - Include comments explaining non-obvious parts
727: - Show complete, runnable examples
728: - Use placeholder values that are obviously placeholders
729: 
730: **Placeholders**:
731: - Format: `[descriptive-name]` or `your-value-here`
732: - Examples:
733:   - ✅ `[skill-name]`, `[feature-description]`, `your-project-name`
734:   - ❌ `xxx`, `placeholder`, `FIXME`
735: 
736: **Lists**:
737: - Use `-` for unordered lists
738: - Use `1.` for ordered lists
739: - Nested lists indent by 2 spaces
740: - Keep items parallel in structure
741: 
742: **Tables**:
743: - Include header row
744: - Align consistently (usually left-aligned)
745: - Keep rows concise (1-2 lines)
746: - Use for comparisons or reference data
747: 
748: ### Writing Style
749: 
750: **Clarity**:
751: - Write for someone unfamiliar with your skill
752: - Define domain-specific terms on first use
753: - Use active voice: "Create the file" not "The file should be created"
754: - Be concise but complete
755: 
756: **Examples**:
757: - Every template should have a complete example
758: - Show real-world usage, not toy examples
759: - Include common variations
760: - Annotate non-obvious parts
761: 
762: **Consistency**:
763: - Use same terminology throughout
764: - Follow patterns from other assets in the skill
765: - Match style of SKILL.md
766: - Use consistent formatting
767:

855: ## 12. ASSET MAINTENANCE
856: 
857: ### When to Update Assets
858: 
859: **Update asset files when**:
860: - New template variations emerge
861: - User feedback reveals confusion
862: - Standards or conventions change
863: - New use cases discovered
864: - Examples become outdated
865: 
866: **Version control**:
867: - Note significant changes in skill version bump
868: - Keep examples current with latest patterns
869: - Remove deprecated templates
870: - Add migration notes for breaking changes
871: 
872: ### Deprecation Strategy
873: 
874: **If removing a template**:
875: 1. Mark as deprecated in section header: `## DEPRECATED: Template Name`
876: 2. Explain why deprecated and what to use instead
877: 3. Keep for 1-2 skill versions (with deprecation warning)
878: 4. Remove after migration period
